items.label: Fig. 1, mean IM of the risk SNPs (40 bars)

assumptions.what: Published bar heights, error bars and curve points read off the PMC figure JPEGs (600 px wide) through each axis's tick marks
assumptions.sensitivity: Tick fits within 0.4 px; one pixel is 0.006 IM in Fig. 1, 0.003 in Fig. 2 and about 0.005 in Figs 3-6, and is added to every tolerance. Curve points where another curve hides the series are not read.

assumptions.what: IM is printed as 100 x the mean decrease in accuracy over trees, as Random Forests 5.1 writes it; Eq. 1 of the paper has a factor 2/T
assumptions.sensitivity: With the factor 2 every IM doubles: our no-LD RF0:IM0 would be 1.31 against the published 0.64, outside the tolerance (0.13). Without it, 0.65.

assumptions.what: RF1 threshold R = 0.5 (the paper does not give it)
assumptions.sensitivity: LD SNPs are perfect proxies (r2 = 1) and noise SNPs correlate by chance up to r2 of about 0.03-0.05, so every R from 0.1 (above the largest chance r2, 0.09, in our replicates) to just below 1 gives the same forests. R = 0.02 also drops chance-correlated noise SNPs; it is in summary.json as RF1(R=0.02) and lowers the risk SNPs' IM0 (see the RF1 cause of Fig. 1).

assumptions.what: The 13 LD models of a replicate are built on the same n0 data set (incremental), for H4M4 as for the other models
assumptions.sensitivity: The paper says it built the other models incrementally; for H4M4 its wording is ambiguous, and its Figs 1-2 n series fall too smoothly for independent data sets. Each LD model on its own data (snp_independent in summary.json) changes no conclusion: Fig. 1 also comes back 40 of 40.

assumptions.what: Cases are the first 250 affected and controls the first 250 unaffected people drawn from the population model (Lunetta et al. 2004 do not say how the samples were drawn)
assumptions.sensitivity: Not tested; drawing controls from the whole population would add about 10% affected people to the controls of H4M4 (K = 0.098).

cause.summary: 30 of 33 bars agree. The paper's PRED.rHAP bars are all the same height (0.654, error bars too): two of them miss ours at r2 = 0 and 0.1, a plotting slip. The rHAP bar at r2 = 0 (0.565 against our 0.736) is the low-r2 gap of Fig. 5.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Monte Carlo noise
hypotheses.test: Fig. 5: rHAP misses at five consecutive r2 levels (0-0.4) by 0.29-0.35 against tolerances of 0.21, all in the same direction

hypotheses.hypothesis: Our rule for the haplotype frequencies (the paper leaves one free)
hypotheses.test: The other rule (T-T = G-C) gives the same flat rHAP: 27 of 33 Fig. 5 bars and 30 of 33 Fig. 4 bars within tolerance, the same misses (comparison.json controls)

hypotheses.hypothesis: The authors' program split the 10-level haplo-genotype as a number (thresholds of its code), not as a category
hypotheses.test: hap_variants.py, 30 replicates: rHAP IM 0.17, 0.20, 0.61 at r2 = 0, 0.5, 1 (categorical 0.72, 0.79, 0.60; paper Fig. 4 0.565, 0.742, 0.654): the right direction at r2 = 0 but far too low at 0.5, where the paper matches the categorical coding

exceptions.evidence: All 11 published PRED.rHAP bars of Fig. 4 have the same top row and the same error bar (0.654 +- 0.079, published_values.json), equal to the rHAP bar at r2 = 1; Fig. 5 shows PRED.rHAP varying from 0.38 to 0.74 over the same data.

page.lede: {items} results: {exact} exact, {agrees} agree, {partly} partly agree, {differs} differs, {not_attempted} not attempted. The lost program was rebuilt from the paper and checked against Breiman and Cutler's Fortran, and the simulations were run again.
page.items_caption: Every figure, table and claim of the paper. A figure value agrees when it is within 3 combined Monte Carlo standard errors and one pixel of the published one.
page.claims_line: The main claim holds for the paper's H4M4 figures and five of the six other models: the revised importance with the original forest is the steadiest under LD. It does not hold for H1M1 (open). Fig. 2's swapped series and Fig. 4's repeated bars are slips in the paper; the low-r2 haplotype gap of Figs 4 to 6 is open.
came_back: Every K, lambda_s and GRR from the model parameters; one GRR is a rounding slip.
All 40 mean importances within Monte Carlo error.
All 40 bars, once two swapped series are put back.
120 of 122 curve points; the two misses sit on vertical jumps.
Random Forests 5.1 with RF1 and IM1, as the Python package rfld, checked against the Fortran original.
buried: Tables 2 to 4: the TGen Alzheimer genotypes were only ever handed out by request.
The threshold R of the revised forest is not in the paper; any R from 0.1 to just below 1 gives the same result here.
Why the paper's true haplotypes do worse at low r2 than the model gives (Figs 4 to 6): three candidate causes ruled out.
page.matched_intro: How each part of the paper's method was rebuilt.
matched: A step-by-step port of Random Forests 5.1 for categorical SNPs, 5000 trees, mtry 35.
A tree drops every SNP with r2 above R with a SNP it already uses.
The permutation importance over the trees that use the SNP.
Lunetta et al.'s heterogeneity-multiplicative models; 100 replicates of 250 cases and 250 controls.
EM phasing as in haplo.stats, 100 sampled phasings with 1000 trees each.
page.closing: Random forests in LD came back from the paper's text, with one program still online to check against.
